Smooth local projections (Barnichon & Brownlees)

Source: R/lp-smooth.R
lp_smooth.Rd

Imposes that the impulse response is a smooth function of the horizon, \(\beta(h) = \sum_{j=1}^J \theta_j B_j(h)\) with a B-spline basis \(B_j\) (cubic by default, equally spaced knots over \(0..H\)), and estimates all horizons jointly by penalised least squares: $$\hat\theta = \arg\min_\theta \sum_{h=0}^H\sum_t \Big(\tilde y_{t+h}-\sum_j\theta_jB_j(h)\tilde s_{t,h}\Big)^2 + \lambda\,\theta'D_r'D_r\theta,$$ where tilde denotes residuals from the horizon-specific regression on the controls (Frisch-Waugh), \(D_r\) is the \(r\)-th order difference matrix (P-spline penalty, Eilers & Marx 1996) which shrinks \(\beta(h)\) towards a polynomial of degree \(r-1\) as \(\lambda\to\infty\). \(\lambda\) is chosen by K-fold cross-validation over contiguous blocks of time (preserving serial dependence). Standard errors use the HAC sandwich \((A+\lambda P)^{-1}\hat\Omega(A+\lambda P)^{-1}\), \(\hat\Omega\) Newey-West on the scores summed over horizons at each \(t\); they treat the smoothing bias as negligible.

Usage

lp_smooth(
  Y,
  shock,
  response = 1L,
  horizon = 20L,
  lags = 4L,
  contemp = NULL,
  controls = NULL,
  cumulative = FALSE,
  nbasis = NULL,
  degree = 3L,
  penalty_order = 2L,
  lambda = NULL,
  nfolds = 5L,
  nw_lag = NULL,
  level = c(0.68, 0.9)
)

Arguments

Y

data frame / tibble / matrix (T x K) of responses (and the source of lag controls). Non-numeric columns (e.g. a date) are dropped.

shock

the shock \(s_t\): a variable of Y (tidyselect; observed shock, unit-impact normalisation) or a numeric vector of length T (external shock series, e.g. narrative).

response

<tidy-select> the single response variable of Y.

horizon

maximum horizon H.

lags

number of lags of Y in the controls (and of an external shock).

contemp

<tidy-select> variables of Y entered contemporaneously as controls. For a recursive (Cholesky) identification with shock a variable of Y, list the variables ordered before the shock.

controls

optional extra T x q matrix of controls.

cumulative

cumulate the response (for variables in differences).

nbasis

number of B-spline basis functions \(J\) (default min(H + 1, 8)).

degree

spline degree.

penalty_order

order \(r\) of the difference penalty.

lambda

a fixed (absolute) penalty; NULL = choose by cross-validation over a grid scaled by \(\mathrm{tr}(A)/J\).

nfolds

number of CV blocks.

nw_lag

Newey-West truncation for the score (default H + 1).

level

confidence levels for the pointwise bands.

Value

an lp_smooth object: $estimate/$se ((H+1) x 1), $bands, $vcov (compatible with lp_supt()), $lp/$lp_se (unsmoothed LP), $lambda, $cv (grid and CV errors), $edf.

Details

Economic intuition. Raw LP estimates are noisy and jagged because every horizon is estimated on its own; theory says responses are smooth (hump-shaped, monotone decay). Smoothing borrows strength across neighbouring horizons, trading a small bias (a hump is flattened if \(\lambda\) is too large) for a large variance reduction, which is what the LP-vs-VAR bias-variance trade-off is about: smooth LP sits between unrestricted LP and a parametric VAR. Pitfalls: sharp features (e.g. an impact jump at \(h=0\), a sudden reversal) are smoothed away; use enough basis functions; the bands are conditional on \(\lambda\), ignoring the CV step; one response at a time.

References

Barnichon, R. and Brownlees, C. (2019) Impulse response estimation by smooth local projections. Review of Economics and Statistics.

See also

Other local projections: autoplot.lpm(), compare_lp_var(), lp(), lp_forecast(), lp_joint(), lp_panel(), lp_state(), lp_supt(), tidy.lpm()

Examples

fit <- lp_smooth(
  yraw,
  shock = rate,
  response = infl,
  horizon = 12,
  lags = 2,
  contemp = c(infl, unemp)
)
round(cbind(smooth = fit$estimate[, 1], raw = fit$lp), 3)
#>    smooth    raw
#> 0   0.011  0.000
#> 1   0.003 -0.059
#> 2  -0.007 -0.062
#> 3  -0.019 -0.032
#> 4  -0.034 -0.022
#> 5  -0.054 -0.008
#> 6  -0.080 -0.015
#> 7  -0.114 -0.043
#> 8  -0.155 -0.075
#> 9  -0.203 -0.168
#> 10 -0.256 -0.276
#> 11 -0.313 -0.378
#> 12 -0.372 -0.455
